title: A ring map which becomes an isomorphism after inverting p is a universal homeomorphism exactly when its kernel is locally nilpotent and every element is bridged by a p-power multiple and a p-power

standard_prerequisites.name: The algebra criterion that a ring map whose kernel is locally nilpotent and which has the stated bridging property gives a universal homeomorphism
standard_prerequisites.use: Gives the easier implication from the algebraic condition to the geometric one.

standard_prerequisites.name: If a morphism of spectra is a universal homeomorphism then the kernel of the corresponding ring map consists of nilpotent elements, cited from the algebra chapter
standard_prerequisites.use: Allows the base ring to be replaced by the image, so that the map is injective.

standard_prerequisites.name: The set of elements bridged by a p-power multiple and a p-power is a subalgebra, cited from the algebra chapter
standard_prerequisites.use: Produces the subalgebra whose equality with the target is what has to be shown.

standard_prerequisites.name: The two-step criterion producing an element outside a subalgebra with either two consecutive powers inside or a prime multiple and a prime power inside, cited from the same chapter
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the element used to derive the contradiction that closes the proof.

core_obligations: Easy direction: the algebraic condition on the kernel and on the bridging of elements implies that the morphism of spectra is a universal homeomorphism by the cited algebra criterion (proof lines 11839-11840).

Reduction to an injective map: assuming the morphism is a universal homeomorphism, its kernel consists of nilpotent elements, so replacing the base ring by the image one may assume the map is injective (proof lines 11841-11844).

Build the candidate subalgebra: the set of elements of the target for which some p-power multiple and some p-power lie in the base is a subalgebra of the target, and the task is to show it is everything (proof lines 11845-11849).

Contradiction: if the subalgebra is proper, the cited criterion produces an element outside it with either two consecutive powers inside or, for some prime, a prime multiple and a prime power inside; since the map becomes an isomorphism after inverting p one may multiply the element by a p-power to land in the base, and in the first case the p-power of the element itself lies in the subalgebra and hence in the base up to a further p-power, giving a contradiction; in the second case the prime involved must be p, because otherwise a p-power multiple and the prime multiple would combine to put the element itself in the subalgebra, and then the same argument applies to the p-power of the element (proof lines 11851-11870).
proof_roadmap: Use the algebra criterion for the easy direction, then reduce to an injective ring map by discarding the nilpotent kernel (proof lines 11839-11844).
Compare the target with the subalgebra of bridged elements and contradict properness using the two-step criterion and the fact that inverting p gives an isomorphism (proof lines 11845-11870).
difficulty_reason: The lemma says that for a ring map which becomes an isomorphism after inverting a prime p, the induced morphism of spectra is a universal homeomorphism exactly when the kernel is locally nilpotent and every element of the target is bridged to the base by a p-power multiple and a p-power (statement lines 11825-11837). The counted proof is short but has real content: it uses an algebra criterion for the easy direction, reduces to an injective map by discarding the nilpotent kernel, forms the subalgebra of bridged elements, and then derives a contradiction from the two-step criterion for a proper subalgebra, in each of the two possible shapes, using that a p-power multiple of any element lands in the base because inverting p gives an isomorphism (proof lines 11839-11870). It is H2: both directions are carried out in the counted span, with the cited inputs being standard criteria for universal homeomorphisms and for subalgebras.
